reason: The text (Numbers 13-14) extensively establishes and reinforces multiple layers of strict hierarchy. God gives direct commands to Moses, who acts as chief mediator and authority figure. The spies are explicitly selected as 'chiefs' (נשיא - leaders) from each tribe—one 'chief of them.' These men are identified as 'heads of the children of Israel,' demonstrating organized hierarchical tribal leadership. Moses and Aaron exercise clear authority in giving commands and reporting, with the congregation obligated to listen to their leadership. When the Israelites rebel against this established hierarchy—complaining against Moses and Aaron and refusing to follow their guidance—they are portrayed negatively and face divine punishment. The narrative shows that resistance to the established hierarchy of God → Moses → Aaron → tribal chiefs → people results in consequences (40 years in the wilderness, death of the rebellious generation). Hierarchy is not only important but essential to the narrative's moral framework.
